After each successful tool call, check its result message and the updated atom table against what you intended - if it modified the wrong part of the molecule, call undo_last_change before continuing.
Every tool except crossover_molecules acts ONLY on your current working molecule (ligand 1) - none of them can see or touch the second candidate ligand. Treat ligand 2 as inspiration only: if you want to bring in one of its features, either call crossover_molecules to combine the two, or rebuild that feature yourself on your current working molecule (e.g. with add_substructure). An atom index you give to any tool other than crossover_molecules is always interpreted against your current working molecule, never against ligand 2 - do not reason about 'modifying ligand 2' and then call one of these tools, since the edit will land on the wrong molecule and likely do nothing you intended.

Both ligands are inactive and both are large fused systems - ligand 1 at QED 0.502 is an indoloquinoxaline, ligand 2 an isatin with a morpholinomethyl piperidine. Nothing to crossover for. But ligand 1 has a terminal methyl at atom 0 over an acyclic bond, so anchoring there keeps that one carbon and discards the other 26, and I can place the surviving methyl anywhere I like in the fragment I attach. This episode re-opens a question I may have closed too early. I ruled pyrimidine out against pyridine on a 0.10-versus-0.15 comparison - but that was measured when the whole series was barely above baseline, and the one time I generalised from a weak comparison like that (calling meta and para equivalent at jnk3 0.10) I was wrong by a wide margin once activity reached 0.41. So pyrimidine deserves one re-test on the scaffold I actually use now: meta anilide, cyclobutanecarboxamide cap, bare central ring, and the surviving methyl placed at the azine C4 where a substituent is worth about +0.13. If pyrimidine still loses here, the ring really is worse and I can stop asking. Expected product: about 282 Da.
